opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting question, because when people hear "world model" they usually think of something very grand: a giant simulator that can generate video, or a robot that plans its actions in a physical environment. But I've started to feel that some of the clearest early signals actually show up in the small, everyday devices we carry around.

Take something like smart glasses, or even an earbud with an always-on assistant. What makes it useful isn't just that it can recognize objects or transcribe what you say. It has to keep some persistent representation of your situation over time: where you are, what you were just looking at, what you're probably trying to do next, how the scene in front of you is likely to change. If I put my keys down and walk away, a truly helpful device should "know" where they are, even though they're no longer in view. That's object permanence. That's a model of the world, not just a perception system.

And I think that's the key distinction. A lot of today's AI is still fundamentally reactive. You give it an input, it gives you an output. A world model is about maintaining an internal state of the environment, predicting how it evolves, and using that to reason or act. Wearables force you into that setting because they live in a continuous, first-person, embodied stream of experience. There's no clean prompt boundary. The data is egocentric, it's multimodal, it's noisy, and it's tied to your actual physical life.

So when I use these devices, I feel two things at the same time. One is excitement, because you can sense the outline of what an assistant with real spatial and temporal understanding could feel like. The other is a kind of frustration, because you also see very clearly where the gap is. The device often doesn't really understand 3D space, it forgets context, it can't anticipate. Those failures are actually very informative. They tell you exactly which capabilities a world model needs to have.

That's partly why I think language alone won't get us there. Language is an amazing compression of human knowledge, but the world isn't made of tokens. A lot of what we understand about space, physics, and cause and effect is learned through seeing and acting, not through reading. Wearables are one of the most natural places where vision, memory, and prediction have to come together, so for me they're almost like a testbed, a window into what the next generation of intelligence needs to look like.

r001.rationale: The response attributes wearables’ world-model potential to continuous, first-person multimodal experience and tracking the surrounding situation. It does not mention continuous monitoring of bodily indicators.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's funny, because I didn't go looking for it. I wear a ring that tracks my sleep, and an app that reads my glucose, and over time I noticed that what these things are actually doing is building an internal model of me. Not just logging numbers. They're predicting. The ring will tell me in the morning, "you're going to feel tired around three o'clock," and it's usually right. The glucose app learns that if I eat rice at this time, my curve will look like this, and it starts anticipating before the data even comes in.

That, to me, is the essence of a world model. A world model isn't just perception, it's not just "what is happening now." It's a compressed representation of how a system evolves, so you can simulate forward and ask, "if I do this, what happens next?" The device has a little simulator of my body running inside it. It's a very narrow world, just one person's physiology, but structurally it's the same idea we talk about in vision and robotics: observe, build state, predict, and then use that prediction to intervene.

And what I find interesting from a research perspective is that these models are learned almost entirely from passive, unlabeled, continuous data. Nobody is annotating my sleep. It's just a long stream of sensor readings, and the structure emerges from predicting the next state. That's exactly the argument we make for self-supervised learning and for why world models should come from video rather than from language. The wearable is a small, slightly boring, but very real existence proof that this works. It's a world model for a world of one.

r001.rationale: The response describes wearables tracking sleep and glucose through continuous sensor readings, from which they learn bodily patterns and make predictions.

astra-6.text:
I think of a wearable as a possible interface to a world model. It moves with you, so it can observe a continuous stream of what you see, what you do, and how your surroundings change. That’s quite different from giving a model one image and asking it to describe it.

The interesting question is whether it can connect those observations over time. Can it remember where you left something? Can it understand that you’re in the middle of an activity, even when the relevant object is no longer visible? And can it anticipate what might happen when you take an action? Those capabilities require some internal understanding of a world that persists beyond the current frame.

So I wouldn’t say a wearable is itself a world model. It provides a way for a model to observe the world continuously and, potentially, learn the relationship between perception, action, and consequences. That’s where I see the connection.

r001.rationale: The response connects wearables to continuous observation of what a person sees and does and how surroundings change, but does not attribute their world-model-like characteristics to monitoring bodily indicators.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of a wearable as a small window into the world. It sees some of what I see, hears some of what I hear, and potentially has context about what I’m doing. But collecting those signals isn’t enough. To be useful, it has to connect them into an understanding of the situation: where I am, what I’m interacting with, and what I might be trying to accomplish.

That’s where I see the connection to world models. If I ask, “Where did I leave my keys?” the device needs more than object recognition. It needs to connect an object to a place and a moment, and maintain that information as I move around. If it’s going to help me take an action, it also needs some understanding of what could happen next.

I wouldn’t say a wearable automatically has a world model. But it creates a very natural setting for one: a continuous stream of partial observations, grounded in someone’s everyday experience, that the system has to make sense of over time.

r001.rationale: The response describes wearables collecting visual, audio, and activity-context signals over time, but does not attribute their world-model-like characteristics to continuous monitoring of bodily indicators.
